history.heading: Peoples and kingdoms
paragraphs: Zambia, in south-central Africa, has been inhabited for a very long time; the Broken Hill skull (Kabwe 1), found in 1921, is about 300,000 years old. Bantu-speaking peoples arrived in the first millennium CE. Kingdoms such as the Lozi (Barotseland), Bemba, Lunda and Chewa developed. In the 19th century, Ngoni and Kololo migrations reshaped the region, and David Livingstone explored it, naming Victoria Falls in 1855.

history.heading: Northern Rhodesia
paragraphs: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took control in the 1890s, and the territory became the British protectorate of Northern Rhodesia in 1924. Rich copper deposits in the Copperbelt made it valuable. In 1953 it was joined with Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland in a federation dominated by white settlers, which was dissolved in 1963.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda, who ruled for 27 years, establishing a one-party state in 1972 and supporting liberation movements in neighbouring countries. Falling copper prices caused economic decline. Multiparty democracy returned in 1991, and Zambia has since had several peaceful transfers of power, most recently in 2021, when Hakainde Hichilema won the presidency.

culture.heading: One Zambia, One Nation
paragraphs: Zambia has over 70 ethnic groups, and its motto is "One Zambia, One Nation". English is official, and Bemba, Nyanja, Tonga and Lozi are widely spoken. Most people are Christian; the constitution declares Zambia a Christian nation.

Traditional ceremonies include the Kuomboka of the Lozi, when the king moves from the flooded plains by royal barge. Nshima, a thick maize porridge, is the staple food. Victoria Falls, shared with Zimbabwe, is one of the world's largest waterfalls.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Zambia is a presidential republic. Since 2021 President Hichilema's United Party for National Development has governed. Debates include debt, the cost of living and concerns over laws affecting free speech. General elections were held in August 2026.

economy.heading: Copper
paragraphs: Zambia is Africa's second-largest copper producer, and copper accounts for most exports; it also produces cobalt and emeralds. The Lobito Corridor railway project aims to improve export routes. Agriculture employs most people, though droughts, such as the severe one in 2024 that also cut hydropower, are a major risk.
Zambia defaulted on its debt in 2020, the first African country to do so during the pandemic, and completed a debt restructuring in 2024. The currency is the kwacha.
